LUREX: Lunar Radiation Environment Explorer

MAE 342 Space System Design · 16-person team · Final Design Review, May 2026

A dual-spacecraft lunar constellation that monitors the radiation environment around the Moon to support future crewed missions, designed within NASA Small Explorer (SMEX) cost limits. LiLO flies a 100 km polar orbit to measure solar energetic particles and galactic cosmic rays near the surface. MiLO flies an 8,000 km orbit to watch the solar wind and Earth's magnetotail. Both ride to trans-lunar injection as ESPA Grande rideshare payloads, then insert themselves into lunar orbit.

Propulsion and Launch Vehicle (PLV) and Power subsystems

  • Propulsion architecture. Led the chemical vs. electric trade. Electric propulsion was rejected because a 5 N electric system needs about 102 kW and a months-long spiral to capture at the Moon, which would break the December 2030 operations deadline.
  • Thruster and propellant selection. Showed that the LOI-class burns need a specific impulse of at least 305 s, which rules out monopropellant engines. Chose a hybrid system: a bipropellant main engine plus hydrazine RCS thrusters sharing one fuel tank. Selected the Agile Space LE144 engine (144 N, 328 s Isp) over the heavier BT-4 because of volume limits.
  • Feed system. Chose a blowdown feed over a pressure-regulated one. It removes the separate pressurant tank and regulator, saving mass, volume and failure points within the 465 kg launch-mass limit.
  • Plume contamination. Reviewed the literature on hydrazine exhaust deposition, confirmed it is negligible above 172 K, and worked with the structures team to keep instruments out of a 12° keep-out cone around each nozzle.
  • Also contributed to tank sizing, the impulsive-burn validation (the longest burn is 5.85% of its orbital period) and the power-distribution loss analysis.

Modeling GPS Coverage with Molniya and GEO Orbits

MAE 341 Space Flight · Individual project in two parts · December 2025

In Part A I rebuilt the 24-satellite NAVSTAR GPS constellation in Ansys STK. I mapped how coverage over the U.S., Australia and the whole globe degrades as satellites are switched off, tracked a moving car with a 13° receiver mask, and modeled launch from Cape Canaveral through a Hohmann transfer to MEO.

In Part B I asked whether fewer, exotic orbits could do the same job. I swapped one orbital plane for a Molniya orbit, then for a GEO satellite, and judged each by satellites in view and position dilution of precision (PDOP). Neither worked. Molniya left high-PDOP zones over the northwestern U.S. and the Pacific. GEO left gaps over North Africa, Southern Europe and Central and Southeast Asia, and had no access at all to southern Australia. Both also cost far more delta-V to reach than a single MEO slot.

Hall Effect Thruster Study: Propellant Injection

Five-person team · Spring 2026

The team pitched an improved Hall thruster against SpaceX's Starlink V2 Mini argon thruster (170 mN, 2,500 s). The pitch combined three changes: solid iodine propellant, an inward-inclined magnetic topology, and a new propellant injection scheme.

I owned the propellant injection analysis

Today's thrusters feed neutral gas axially through the anode, so ionization bunches near the channel centerline and some neutrals escape un-ionized. I compared that baseline against inner-wall, outer-wall and combined radial injection. Injecting from both walls gave the most uniform ionization probability across the channel and the lowest neutral density downstream, without giving up propellant utilization.

Search and Rescue Robot (S.a.R.R.): Bulkhead

MAE 322 Mechanical Design · 11-person team · Fall 2025

Bulkhead is an autonomous robot built to climb a 15° ramp, thread a doglegged chute, breach a two-step 1 ft wall and drop a 1 kg medkit at a victim. Its design centers on two 24-inch drive wheels, chosen so it can climb the wall by simply driving over it.

Manufacturing, wheel hub design and rear platform design

  • Machined parts on CNC mills, manual mills and lathes, and drew structural and drivetrain parts in Creo.
  • Redesigned the wheel hubs after the original PLA axle mounts sheared under drive torque. The final hubs are machined from scrap aluminum.
  • Designed the 1.75 lb acrylic rear platform, about 6% of total mass. A test piece cracked when dropped with the motor mounted, so I added two 6061 aluminum T-brackets, and the platform then survived the 1 ft drop seen after the wall.

At the final demo Bulkhead cleared the ramp and chute under open-loop control. Belt slip at the wall and drivetrain delays kept the team from a full autonomous run. Both problems are traced in the report.

Wing Project

MAE 321 · Eight-person team

The task was a riveted aluminum wing that carries 95.5 lb applied 23 inches from the root while staying as light and stiff as possible. The airfoil shape was fixed, but its taper, the spar, bulkheads, skin and rivet pattern were open. We optimized each part on its own in Creo FEA under a 100 lbf tip load, then integrated, built and load-tested the wing to failure.

Skin design (co-lead with Ani Kozak)

A 0.03 in skin deflected more than 1 inch in every material combination, so I moved to 0.04 in. I then compared 6061-T6 and 7075-T6 skins top and bottom. A stiffer 7075 bottom skin saved only 0.01 in of deflection and pushed high stress into the end bulkheads, so I chose 0.04 in 6061-T6 for both surfaces. The FEA showed about 25 ksi peak stress and 0.90 in deflection.

Weight Rack Design

Individual project

The brief was a rack under 250 lb that holds 295 lb of plates: four 45s, two 25s, four 10s and five 5s. I dropped the usual upright "tree" design for a low, floor-bolted steel frame. It keeps the center of gravity near the ground and reduces bending in the holds. The large plates lean between three triangular holds made from two angle-cut pipes welded together, and the small plates sit on two end posts.

Two changes came out of the assembly model. I lengthened the base plate from 20 to 25 inches so the side plates fit, and I moved the corner posts to the centerline after the stacked plates collided. A static analysis of the most heavily loaded hold confirmed the design with a wide margin. The rack is designed to be built with a manual mill, lathe and TIG welder.
